To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
acclimation to repeated decompression cycles reduces the expression of inflammatory and stress response genes in the lung and the incidence of DCS.
exposure to repeated compression and decompression (9 dives) resulted in acclimation of rats to a subsequent decompression dive.
acclimated animals have a decreased susceptibility to DCS and have decreased expression of inflammatory and stress-related cytokine genes compared with animals without prior acclimation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an animal model for acclimation to compression-decompression.
the molecular mechanisms associated acclimation to compression-decompression.

the molecular and cellular events associated with the initiation and progression to decompression sickness and the potential role of repeated compression-decompression exposure in reducing susceptibility to decompression sickness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular mechanisms associated to acclimation to repeated decompression are still unclear and need further studies to elucidate the molecular mechanisms associated.
this study suggests that activation ERK1/ 2 and upregulating the expression of Egr- 1 and its target genes by rapid decompressions may be involved in the initiation and progressions of DCS.
acclimation to repetitive decompression results in an upregulation of genes involved in the acute inflammatory response to decompression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

acclimation to repeated compression/decompression stress may be associated with a downregulation of the stress response and inflammatory gene expression in lung tissue, which may be associated with reduced susceptibility to DCS.
acclimation is a complex process involving both the up and down regulation of genes and that the down-regulation of genes is associated with acclimated animals with DCS.
acclimation to repeated decompression stress may result in an upregulated anti-inflammatory and stress response and a downregulated inflammatory response in the lungs of animals with DCS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
acclimation to compression-decompression stress is associated with changes in gene expression and signal pathways that are involved in stress and inflammatory processes.
acclimation to repeated compression-depression cycles is associated with reduced expression of genes that may play a role during the onset of decompression sickness.
repeated compression-decompression exposure may lead to downregulation of genes involved in the inflammatory response to decompression.
